abstract: SUMMARY Both subunit and attenuated whole-sporozoite vaccination strategies against Plasmodium infection have shown promising initial results in malaria-naive westerners but less efficacy in malaria-exposed individuals in endemic areas. Here, we demonstrate proof of concept by using a rodent malaria model in which non-neutralizing antibodies (nNAbs) can directly interfere with protective anti-circumsporozoite protein (CSP) humoral responses. We characterize a monoclonal antibody, RAM1, against Plasmodium yoelii sporozoite major surface antigen CSP. Unlike the canonical Py CSP repeat domain binding and neutralizing antibody (NAb) 2F6, RAM1 does not inhibit sporozoite traversal or entry of hepatocytes in vitro or infection in vivo . Although 2F6 and RAM1 bind non-overlapping regions of the CSP-repeat domain, pre-treatment with RAM1 abrogates the capacity of NAb to block sporozoite traversal and invasion in vitro . Importantly, RAM1 reduces the efficacy of the polyclonal humoral response against Py CSP in vivo . Collectively, our data provide a proof of concept that nNAbs can alter the efficacy of malaria vaccination.

EXPERIMENTAL MODEL AND SUBJECT DETAILS
Cell lines and cell culture
In vitro
, Hepa1–6 cells were used for
P. yoelii
infections. Cells were maintained in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) complete media (Cellgro), supplemented with 10% FBS (Sigma-Aldrich), 100IU/ml penicillin (Cellgro), 100mg/ml streptomycin (Cellgro), and 2.5mg/ml Fungizone (HyClone/Thermo Fisher).
Experimental animals
Female Swiss Webster (SW) mice, 6–10 weeks of age, were purchased from Envigo. Female BALB/cJ mice, 6–8 weeks of age, were purchased from The Jackson Laboratory. Mice were housed under standard housing conditions and fed
ad libitum
water and food. Blood was collected by sub-mandibular, chin or cardiac puncture. All animal protocols were performed according to protocols reviewed by the Seattle Children’s Research Institute IACUC.
Mosquito rearing and sporozoite production
P. yoelii
wild-type strain 17XNL (BEI resources) was maintained in Swiss Webster mice (Envigo). Swiss Webster mice were injected intraperitoneal (IP) with 250 μL of infected blood at 3%–5% parasitemia. Gametocyte exflagellation rate was checked 4 days post-injection. Mice were then anesthetized with 150 μL Ketamine Xylazine solution (12.5 mg/mL ketamine, 1.25 mg/mL xylazine in PBS) and naive female Anopheles stephensi mosquitoes (3–7 days old) were allowed to feed on them. Mosquitoes were maintained at 23°C and 80% humidity with a 12L-12D light cycle. On day 10, the midguts from ten mosquitoes are dissected and oocysts counted as a measure of infection. On day 15 post-infection, mosquitoes are used for mosquito bite challenge or are dissected to isolate salivary glands and extract sporozoites.

5

Douglass et al., 2015

Traversal assay
Freshly isolated sporozoites were exposed to 2F6 or RAM1 or 50C1 antibodies either alone or in combinations for 10 mins at indicated concentrations. 5 × 10
5
HFF-1 cells were seeded in each well of a 24-well plate (Corning). Cells were exposed to antibody treated sporozoites and high molecular mass Dextran-FITC (70 kDa) (Sigma) for 90 mins. Cells were harvested with accutase (Life technologies) and fixed with Cytoperm/Cytofix (BD Biosciences). Cells were blocked with Perm/Wash (BD Biosciences) supplemented with 2% BSA for 1 h at room temperature then stained overnight at 4°C with Alexa fluor 488-conjugated CSP antibodies to CSP-. The cells were then washed and resuspended in PBS with 5 mM EDTA. Invasion rate and dextran uptake (traversal) were measured by flow cytometry on a LSRII (Becton Dickinson) and analyzed by FlowJo (Tree Star).
Immunofluorescence
Freshly isolated sporozoites were exposed to 2F6 Alexa Fluor 405, RAM1-Alexa Fluor 594 or 50C1-Alexa Fluor 488 antibodies either alone or in pairwise combinations for 10 mins together or sequentially at indicated concentrations. Sporozoites were spun at 17000
g
for 5 mins and washed with 1xPBS-EDTA and fixed with 3.7% PFA for 20 mins. Sporozoites were transferred to 8-well chambered slides and the images were acquired with a 100 × 1.4 NA objective (Olympus) on a DeltaVision Elite High-Resolution Microscope (GE Healthcare Life Sciences). The sides of each pixel represent 64.5 × 64.5 nm and z stacks were acquired at 300 nm intervals. Approximately 5–15 slices were acquired per image stack. For deconvolution, the 3D datasets were processed to remove noise and reassign blur by an iterative Classic Maximum Likelihood Estimation widefield algorithm provided by Huygens Professional Software (Scientific Volume Imaging, the Netherlands).
QUANTIFICATION AND STATISTICAL ANALYSIS
Statistical significance was determined with a one-way ANOVA with multiple comparisons or two-tailed unpaired Student’s t test. Analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism version 8 for Windows. For the Kaplan–Meier curves, comparisons were tested using the log-rank test. Statistical tests used, what n represents, and precision measures can be found in figure legends.

After 90 mins of infection, cells were harvested with accutase (Life technologies) and fixed with Cytoperm/Cytofix (BD Biosciences). Cells were blocked with Perm/Wash (BD Biosciences) + 2% BSA for 1 h at room temperature then stained overnight at 4°C with antibodies to CSP-Alexafluor 488 conjugate. The cells were then washed and resuspended in PBS-containing 5 mM EDTA. Infection rate was measured by flow cytometry (
Douglass et al., 2015
) on an LSRII (Becton Dickinson) and analyzed by FlowJo (Tree Star).
Traversal assay
Freshly isolated sporozoites were exposed to 2F6 or RAM1 or 50C1 antibodies either alone or in combinations for 10 mins at indicated concentrations. 5 × 10
5
HFF-1 cells were seeded in each well of a 24-well plate (Corning). Cells were exposed to antibody treated sporozoites and high molecular mass Dextran-FITC (70 kDa) (Sigma) for 90 mins. Cells were harvested with accutase (Life technologies) and fixed with Cytoperm/Cytofix (BD Biosciences). Cells were blocked with Perm/Wash (BD Biosciences) supplemented with 2% BSA for 1 h at room temperature then stained overnight at 4°C with Alexa fluor 488-conjugated CSP antibodies to CSP-. The cells were then washed and resuspended in PBS with 5 mM EDTA. Invasion rate and dextran uptake (traversal) were measured by flow cytometry on a LSRII (Becton Dickinson) and analyzed by FlowJo (Tree Star).
Immunofluorescence
Freshly isolated sporozoites were exposed to 2F6 Alexa Fluor 405, RAM1-Alexa Fluor 594 or 50C1-Alexa Fluor 488 antibodies either alone or in pairwise combinations for 10 mins together or sequentially at indicated concentrations. Sporozoites were spun at 17000
g
for 5 mins and washed with 1xPBS-EDTA and fixed with 3.7% PFA for 20 mins. Sporozoites were transferred to 8-well chambered slides and the images were acquired with a 100 × 1.4 NA objective (Olympus) on a DeltaVision Elite High-Resolution Microscope (GE Healthcare Life Sciences). The sides of each pixel represent 64.5 × 64.5 nm and z stacks were acquired at 300 nm intervals. Approximately 5–15 slices were acquired per image stack. For deconvolution, the 3D datasets were processed to remove noise and reassign blur by an iterative Classic Maximum Likelihood Estimation widefield algorithm provided by Huygens Professional Software (Scientific Volume Imaging, the Netherlands).

INTRODUCTION
Plasmodium
parasites, the causative agents of malaria, are complex pathogens that have co-evolved with the human host.
Plasmodium
infection of mammals begins with injection of the sporozoite (SPZ) stage parasite into the skin by the bite of an infected
Anopheles
mosquito (
Mota et al., 2001
;
Mota and Rodriguez, 2001
). The sporozoite surface is predominantly coated with the circumsporozoite protein (CSP). Antibodies against CSP are both the goal of the only licensed malaria vaccine RTS/S AS01(
Olotu et al., 2016
;
Stoute et al., 1997
) and found in exposed individuals within endemic areas (
Tapchaisri et al., 1983
;
Triller et al., 2017
). Sporozoites traverse multiple cells in the skin prior to entering a capillary, which facilitates carriage of the sporozoite to the liver (
Ishino et al., 2004
;
Mota et al., 2001
;
Mota and Rodriguez, 2001
,
2002
). Once in the liver, sporozoites traverse the sinusoidal endothelium, entering and exiting liver-resident macrophages and liver sinusoidal endothelial cells, and infect hepatocytes (
Ishino et al., 2005
;
Mota et al., 2001
;
Mota and Rodriguez, 2001
). Within hepatocytes, they develop as liver-stage (LS) parasites for the next 2–10 days (
Prudêncio et al., 2006
;
Shortt et al., 1948
) without eliciting symptoms. This pre-erythrocytic stage of
Plasmodium
is a prime target for vaccine development (
Yamauchi et al., 2007
), as blocking the parasite at this stage would prevent not only disease progression and related symptoms but also subsequent transmission, thereby breaking the parasite life cycle. The development of pre-erythrocytic vaccines is particularly crucial for
Plasmodium vivax
and
Plasmodium ovale
, which have unique latent forms of the parasite in the liver called hypnozoites that initiate relapse infections (
Mueller et al., 2009
). After extensive replication within the hepatocyte, parasites exit the liver and re-enter the bloodstream as merozoites and infect erythrocytes (reviewed in
Prudêncio et al., 2006
). During blood-stage infection, parasites undergo asexual cycles of replication, with each replicative cycle resulting in the destruction of an erythrocyte and the release of additional infectious merozoites. These destructive cycles cause all disease-related symptoms in the human host.
To date, the most advanced malaria vaccine candidate is RTS,S/AS01, a subunit vaccine that elicits high titers of antibodies against CSP. It consists of a portion of the central repeat domain and the C-terminal domain of
Pf
CSP along with CD4 epitope (
Charoenvit et al., 1991
;
Coppi et al., 2011
;
Hollingdale et al., 1984
;
Potocnjak et al., 1980
;
Stewart et al., 1986
). Previous work using rodent, monkey, and human malaria models has demonstrated that CSP monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) partially protect the host from pre-erythrocytic infection (
Epstein et al., 2011
;
Hoffman et al., 2002
). Antibody maturation appears to be one key, as potent neutralization is linked to the affinity and avidity of the antibodies to CSP (
Epstein et al., 2011
;
Jongo et al., 2018
;
Sissoko et al., 2017
). It has been shown that the protection relies on the amount and specificity of the anti-CSP antibodies transferred to the host (
Aliprandini et al., 2018
;
Julien and Wardemann, 2019
;
Kisalu et al., 2018
;
Murugan et al., 2018
;
Tan et al., 2018
;
Triller et al., 2017
). Anti-CSP antibodies are most effective in the skin, where they can render the sporozoite immobile and halt the parasite upstream of the invasion process (
Aliprandini et al., 2018
;
Yamauchi et al., 2007
). Monoclonal Abs to the N and C terminus are less effective at inhibiting sporozoites in the skin, as CSP is N-terminally processed in the mosquito host and undergoes a reversible conformational change to mask some epitopes in the N- and C-terminal domains until the sporozoite interacts with the hepatocyte (
Coppi et al., 2005
;
Herrera et al., 2015
). Furthermore, an epitope target at the R1/Repeat region boundary of CSP has been identified as a site of vulnerability (
Kisalu et al., 2018
). Intriguingly, several CSP-based immunization protocols failed to protect immunized humans in endemic regions despite eliciting high levels of anti-CSP antibodies (
Collins et al., 1989
;
Lal et al., 1987
;
Sedegah et al., 1990
), hinting at a disconnect between the functionality of mAbs and vaccine-induced polyclonal antibodies.
Although these factors hint at what a desirable vaccine-elicited antibody response may need to look like, it also implies that much of the antibody response may be ineffective or irrelevant. In contrast to mAbs, the vaccine-elicited B cell response against CSP is complex and consists of numerous antibody specificities, both neutralizing and non-neutralizing. It is unknown what effect these so-called irrelevant, non-neutralizing antibodies (nNAbs) have on vaccine efficacy (VE) or how their pre-existence in endemic areas may interfere with the function of vaccine-elicited neutralizing antibodies (NAbs). Using the rodent malaria model
Plasmodium yoelii
17XNL, we characterized how the presence of nNAbs impacts the protective efficacy of NAbs against CSP. Although there are potential implications for VE, our focus was on examining the direct interplay between anti-CSP nNAbs and NAbs to determine whether the presence of nNAbs affected the ability of NAbs to neutralize or inhibit the parasite. Our findings implicate direct antibody interference as a mechanism by which pre-existing nNAbs interfere with potent, vaccine-elicited NAbs to reduce VE.
RESULTS
Isolation and generation of RAM1
CSP is a complex protein with multiple unique domains and long stretches of repetitive motifs. The structural organization of CSP is conserved among
Plasmodium
species despite divergence in primary sequence and consists of an N-terminal domain containing a proteolytical cleavage site, a variable central repeat domain, and a C-terminal domain containing a thrombospondin-like type-1 repeat region. The repeat regions consist of major and minor repeat units that can slightly differ within the molecule and structurally appear to be spiral shaped with a specific chirality (
Oyen et al., 2018
). This unique structure enables an unusual binding profile to repeat antibodies, for which it has been reported that up to eight antibody molecules (with a combined molecular mass of ~1,200 kDa) can bind to a single molecule of
Pf
CSP (approximately 70 kDa) (
Fisher et al., 2017
;
Oyen et al., 2017
,
2020
). Thus, CSP antibody binding and neutralization are complex, with the possibility of multiple types of antibodies interacting with a single molecule. Although there is heterogeneity in the primary organization of the CSP repeat region among
Plasmodium
species, immunization with
P. yoelii
CSP (
Py
CSP) generated both NAbs and nNAbs (
Charoenvit et al., 1991
;
Cochrane et al., 1982
;
Hollingdale et al., 1984
;
Nardin et al., 1982
;
Stewart et al., 1986
;
Yoshida et al., 1980
). NAbs targeting the central repeat region of CSP are known to immobilize species-specific SPZs and inhibit their infectivity both
in vitro
(
Hollingdale et al., 1984
;
Stewart et al., 1986
) and
in vivo
(
Charoenvit et al., 1991
;
Cochrane et al., 1982
;
Nardin et al., 1982
;
Yoshida et al., 1980
). To better understand how NAbs and nNAbs target SPZs, we used a rodent malaria model,
Py
CSP, as it allowed us to perform
in vivo
experiments in a robust model system that closely mimics human malaria infection; vaccination with
Py
CSP provides partial protection in malaria-naive BALB/cJ mice, just as RTS,S, which generates a humoral response against
Pf
CSP, provides partial protection in a human challenge model (
Olotu et al., 2016
;
RTS,S Clinical Trials Partnership, 2015
). 2F6 is a prototypical anti-
Py
CSP Nab (
Bruna-Romero et al., 2004
;
Sack et al., 2014
) and binds the
Py
CSP repeat region. 2F6 confers protection in
in vitro
inhibition of
Py
sporozoite infection (ISI) experiments and in passive immunization experiments followed by
Py
-infected mosquito-bite challenge
in vivo
(
Harupa et al., 2014
;
Sack et al., 2014
).
To characterize anti-CSP antibody-mediated protection in more depth, we sought to isolate new anti-
Py
CSP mAbs with properties that differ from the canonical NAb 2F6. We immunized BALB/cJ mice with recombinant
Py
CSP protein (
Py
CSP[NXA]), where NXA denotes that the
N-
linked glycosylation sequence (NXS/T) was mutated to NXA by substitution of alanine for serine and threonine at positions 27 and 348 to prevent the post-translational addition of
N-
linked glycans that are not present on native parasite proteins. After multiple rounds of immunization, we sorted antigen-positive, class-switched memory B cells (MBCs) by using
Py
CSP [NXA] as B cell tetramer bait (
Carbonetti et al., 2017
;
Figure 1A
). The immunoglobulin heavy chain variable (IgHV) and immunoglobulin Kappa variable (IgKV) regions were amplified by RT-PCR and cloned into our expression backbone for recombinant antibody expression in HEK293 cells. We have assembled a library of antibodies with heavy and light chain rearrangements and third complementarity determining regions (CDR3s) that are unique from 2F6. For this study, we choose to investigate the activity of one of the antibodies, RAM1. 2F6 uses IgHV9–2-1*01 and IgKV8–30*01, whereas RAM1 uses the variable genes IgHV1–81*01 and IgKV8–30*01. Although the light chain IgKV gene use is the same, they bear different J segments and CDR3s.
RAM1 and 2F6 exhibit distinct binding kinetics to CSP
Both RAM1 and 2F6 bound to
Py
CSP[NXA] (
Figure 1B
). RAM1 bound with an half maximal effective concentration (EC
50
) of 0.026 μg/ml, whereas 2F6 bound with an EC
50
of 0.0093 μg/ml, indicating that 2F6 bound more tightly by an order of magnitude. We also assessed binding by real-time kinetics by using Octet, a bio-layer interferometry (BLI) method, enabling us to quantify on and off rates (
Figure 1C
). 2F6 binds to
Py
CSP[NXA] with nanomolar affinity of 1.202 × 10
−9
M in a 1:1 binding model, consisting of a fast k
on
(9.804×10
−4
1/Ms) and a very slow k
off
(1.179×10
−3
1/s) (
Figure 1C
). Thus, 2F6 quickly associates and dissociates slowly, if at all. This high-affinity kinetic profile is likely the genesis of its potent neutralizing activity, as affinity of anti-CSP mAbs is associated with neutralization in
Plasmodium falciparum
(
Murugan et al., 2018
). In contrast, when compared with 2F6, RAM1 binds to
Py
CSP[NXA] with more than a log
10
lower affinity (~2.66 × 10
−8
M) (
Figure 1C
). The binding profile does not fit well with a 1:1 binding model, indicating a higher stoichiometry of RAM1 binding CSP. RAM1 exhibits a relatively fast association rate (k
on
= −6.565 3 10
−4
1/Ms) but also has a fast dissociation rate (k
off
= −1.75 × 10
−3
1/s). The negative-control mAb 50C1, which specifically binds to
Pf
TRAP with high affinity, exhibited no binding to
Py
TRAP and was used as an isotype control in subsequent experiments (
Figure S1
). Together, these data demonstrate that RAM1 associates relatively quickly but also dissociates quickly, resulting in a lower overall affinity than 2F6.
To further dissect the binding properties of these two mAbs, we created fragment antibodies (Fabs) by papain digestion. The digested Fabs contain only a single Fv fragment with one heavy and one light chain fragment linked by a disulfide bond, preventing any bivalent binding or avidity effects. 2F6.Fab bound
Py
CSP [NXA] with a K
D
of 5.24 × 10
−7
M (
Figure 2A
) and with an association and dissociation kinetics values of k
on
(9.804 × 10
4
1/Ms) and k
off
(−1.179 × 10
3
1/s). In contrast, RAM1.Fab bound weakly to
Py
CSP[NXA] (
Figure 2B
), and as a result, we were unable to derive a measurable K
D
. This finding suggests that the binding of RAM1 may be dependent on avidity effects. Thus, 2F6 stably binds to
Py
CSP[NXA] with high affinity in a kinetic model that fits a 1:1 binding ratio, which was confirmed by kinetic measurements as a Fab. In contrast, RAM1 binding did not fit a 1:1 binding model, and when evaluated as a Fab, it lost almost all of its reactivity with
Py
CSP[NXA]. Taken together, these data indicate that 2F6 and RAM1 recognize
Py
CSP[NXA] fundamentally differently, both in basic affinity and in potential binding modality. As these studies were conducted
in vitro
with recombinant
Py
CSP[NXA], we next evaluated 2F6 and RAM1 binding to
Py
CSP in its native form on the surface of the sporozoite. We stained
P. yoelii
sporozoites with 2F6 conjugated to AlexaFluor-405 and RAM1 conjugated with AlexaFluor-594. An AlexaFluor-488 conjugate of 50C1 was used as a control. As expected, 50C1 did not bind to
P. yoelii
sporozoites. In contrast, RAM1 and 2F6 exhibited circumferential binding to
P. yoelii
sporozoites, consistent with binding to CSP (
Figure 2C
).
RAM1 and 2F6 recognize non-overlapping epitopes within the central repeat domain of CSP
Py
CSP is a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored protein consisting of several different domains that are thought to have functionality at different points during the parasite’s path to the liver (
Swearingen et al., 2016
). The protein is organized into domains consisting of the N-terminal region, the R1 conserved junctional region, a central repeat domain, the R2 region, and the C-terminal region with highly conserved Thrombospondin type 1 repeats (TSRs). To identify the binding sites of RAM1 and 2F6, we created domain deletion constructs lacking N-terminal
Py
CSP [ΔN] and C-terminal domains
Py
CSP[ΔC]. A third domain mutant was created that contains both the N-terminal and C-terminal domain, connected by two major repeat units
Py
CSP[N2rC] (
Figure 3A
). We tested the binding efficiency of the mAbs RAM1, 2F6, and 50C1 to all domain variants (
Figure 3B
). Both 2F6 and RAM1 bound to full-length
Py
CSP,
Py
CSP[ΔN], and
Py
CSP[ΔC] constructs, suggesting that both mAbs bind to an epitope within the central repeat region that is common to each construct. RAM1 also bound to
Py
CSP[N2rC], which contains two major repeat motifs, whereas 2F6 did not (
Figure 3B
). Thus, both mAbs bind the repeat regions but appear to have different specific epitopes.
Py
CSP has a large number of repeat units consisting of two motifs, namely, the proximal major repeat (QGPGAP; 18 repeating units) and distal minor repeat (QQPP; 6 repeating units) separated by a 4-amino acid spacer sequence, QEPP (
Figures 3A
and
3C
). This arrangement is analogous to
Pf
CSP, which also has major and minor repeat motifs, although the specific amino acid sequences are different (
Coppi et al., 2005
). To map the specific binding of RAM1 and 2F6 within the repeat motifs, we synthesized a series of peptides that spanned different regions within the
Py
CSP repeat region (
Figure 3C
). 2F6 bound peptides spanning the minor repeat (QQPP) but did not bind to any of the peptides spanning the major repeats (
Figure 3D
). 2F6 binding to minor repeat peptides was similar in magnitude to that of full-length
Py
CSP[NXA], indicating that the entire epitope was likely captured by minor repeat peptides. In contrast, RAM1 bound peptides spanning the proximal major repeat region (QGPGAP) and had no reactivity to peptides spanning the minor repeat region (
Figure 3D
). These results are consistent with the finding that RAM1, but not 2F6, binds
Py
CSP[N2rC], which contains two major repeat units and no minor repeats. Interestingly, RAM1 bound major repeat peptides with a lower affinity than the binding to
Py
CSP[NXA]. Thus, either the epitope is more complex than can be presented by the peptide, or a subset of the interactions that mediate RAM1 binding could not be replicated by a linear peptide.
To evaluate if RAM1 and 2F6 biochemically compete for the same epitopes on
Py
CSP[NXA], we performed BLI by using
Py
CSP[NXA]-coated streptavidin biosensors (SA-probe). The antigen-derivatized probes were sequentially incubated with binary combinations of 2F6, RAM1, and 50C1. Binding between RAM1 and
Py
CSP[NXA] was not diminished in the presence of 2F6, nor was binding between
Py
CSP[NXA] and 2F6 diminished by the presence of RAM1. As expected 50C1, the non-binding control antibody, did not bind to
Py
CSP[NXA] (
Figure S2
). To further interrogate the possibility of direct interaction of RAM1 with 2F6, biotinylated-minor repeat-containing peptide (peptide 3) was loaded onto the SA-probe until saturation. The peptide-bound probe was incubated in buffer-containing 2F6 followed by incubation in RAM1 antibody. The presence of RAM1 did not affect the ability of 2F6 to bind the minor repeat peptide, demonstrating there is no direct interaction between the two antibodies (
Figure S3
). Together, these findings illustrate that RAM1 and 2F6 do not directly interact with one another but rather recognize different repeat regions within
Py
CSP[NXA] and that their epitopes are not overlapping.
RAM1 does not neutralize
P. yoelii
sporozoite infection
After deposition in the skin during the probing of an
Anopheles
mosquito, sporozoites must leave the dermis and enter a capillary to survive and further develop. To do this, sporozoites make use of their specialized capacity to traverse cells by using a perforin-like mechanism (
Ishino et al., 2005
). Although the sporozoite can traverse any cell type in a cell-type-independent manner, the dermis is enriched for fibroblasts. Thus, we chose to assess the fibroblast traversal ability of sporozoites in the presence of RAM1. Specifically, we incubated freshly isolated
P. yoelii
wild-type sporozoites with different concentrations (1, 5, and 10 μg) of RAM1, 2F6, or 50C1 antibodies for 10 mins and allowed sporozoites to traverse human foreskin fibroblast (HFF-1) cells for 90 mins in the presence of high-molecular-mass dextran (70 kDa). The dextran-positive cells are wounded cells and were quantified using flow cytometry. We observed no significant differences between the traversal rate of fibroblasts in the presence of RAM1. As expected, we observed a decrease in traversal in the presence of 2F6, a known anti-CSP NAb (
Figure 4A
). Next, we asked whether RAM1 interferes with the infection of hepatocytes. We infected Hepa 1–6 cells for 90 mins with
P. yoelii
sporozoites pre-incubated for 10 mins with different concentrations (1, 5, and 10 μg) of RAM1, 2F6, or 50C1 (
Figure 4B
). We observed no significant differences in the invasion of hepatocytes by RAM1 or 50C1 pre-treated sporozoites. In contrast, we observed a dose-dependent decrease in hepatocyte entry in the presence of 2F6. This result suggests that, unlike 2F6, RAM1 does not alter the traversal and invasion by
P. yoelii
sporozoites.
We next assessed the capacity of RAM1 to alter sporozoite infectivity
in vivo
. BALB/cJ mice were injected intraperitoneally with 150 μg of RAM1, 50C1, or 2F6. After 24 h, mice were challenged with
P. yoelii
-infected mosquitoes. Patency was evaluated beginning 4 days after infection and continued through 14 days post-challenge. Nearly all naive and 50C1-treated mice were infected within 6 days of challenge (
Figure 4C
;
Table S2
). Consistent with the observations of others (
Sack et al., 2014
), we observed a 50% protection in mice that were passively infused with 2F6. Consistent with the
in vitro
results, RAM1 treatment resulted in 100% infection within 6 days of infection. RAM1 did not sterilize the infection even at 500 μg (data not shown), confirming it is a nNAb. Taken together, these data illustrate that RAM1 binds
P. yoelii
CSP but does not affect its capacity to traverse or infect cells
in vitro
or
in vivo
.
RAM1 reduces the inhibitory activity of 2F6
in vitro
We next asked if RAM1 could affect the anti-parasitic activity of the anti-CSP NAb 2F6. We pre-incubated
P. yoelii
sporozoites with pairwise combinations of 2F6, RAM1, and the non-
P. yoelii
-binding negative-control mAb 50C1. We then assessed the traversal of HFF-1 fibroblasts (
Figure 5A
). Interestingly, the concurrent exposure of sporozoites to 2F6 and 50C1 significantly inhibited sporozoite traversal. In contrast, concurrently treating sporozoites with a mixture containing equal amounts of RAM1 and 2F6, or a 5:1 excess of RAM1, resulted in traversal rates similar to those of untreated sporozoites (
Figure 5A
). This finding suggests that the presence of RAM1, whether in equal amounts or in excess, was sufficient to significantly reduce the capacity of 2F6 to inhibit sporozoite traversal.
In contrast, the presence of RAM1 in equal amounts did not affect the hepatocyte invasion inhibitory activity of 2F6 (
Figure 5B
). Concurrent treatment of sporozoites with equal amounts of RAM1 and 2F6 exhibited similar levels of hepatocyte invasion, compared to 2F6–50C1 combination treatment. Consistent with traversal, concurrent treatment of RAM1 and 50C1 exhibited levels of hepatocyte entry similar to those of uninhibited sporozoites, reflecting the non-neutralizing activity of RAM1 (
Figure 5B
). However, when RAM1 was added concurrently in a 5:1 excess, it completely inhibited the invasion blocking activity of 2F6. Thus, the presence of RAM1 ablated the anti-traversal activity of 2F6, whereas hepatocyte invasion blocking was ablated only when RAM1 was present in excess. To further dissect the interference capacity of RAM1, we sequentially pre-incubated sporozoites with combinations of RAM1, 2F6, and 50C1 for 10 mins each and then assessed traversal of HFF-1 fibroblasts (
Figure 5C
) and infection of Hepa 1–6 cells (
Figure 5D
). Pre-treatment of sporozoites with 2F6 followed by treatment of RAM1 or 50C1 reduced sporozoite traversal of fibroblasts (
Figure 5C
) and entry of hepatocytes (
Figure 5D
) at similar levels to those of 2F6 alone. In contrast, pre-treatment with RAM1 (10 or 50 μg), followed by 2F6 (10 μg) led to a significant impairment in the capacity of 2F6 to inhibit fibroblast traversal or hepatocyte invasion (
Figure 5C
,
D
). Thus, if present prior to 2F6, RAM1 was able to completely prevent 2F6 from neutralizing the sporozoite.
We next assessed the capacity of RAM1 to alter the protective efficacy of 2F6
in vivo
. BALB/cJ mice were injected intraperitoneally with 150 μg of RAM1, 2F6, or RAM1+2F6 or with the non-binding 50C1 mAb, as a control. After 24 h, mice were challenged by bite with
P. yoelii
-infected mosquitoes. Blood-stage patency was assessed beginning 4 days after infection and continued through 14 days of post-challenge. Concurrent treatment of RAM1 and 2F6 significantly inhibited the capacity of 2F6 to block infection (
Figure 5E
;
Table S3
), when compared to 2F6 alone. Together, these findings imply that vaccine-elicited anti-CSP NAbs could be ineffective against hepatocyte infection if nNAbs were also present, as seen in pre-existing immunity, particularly if they are present in excess of any vaccine-elicited NAbs.
Next, we tested the capacity of RAM1 to alter the inhibition elicited by polyclonal sera from
Py
CSP[NXA]-immunized BALB/cJ mice. Incubation with serum from immunized mice at a 1:10 dilution significantly inhibited sporozoite invasion in Hepa 1–6 hepatocytes (
Figure 5F
). This inhibition was reversed when RAM1 was added prior to the addition of serum. Together, the data suggest that RAM1 can block the efficacy of not only mAb-blocking activity but also activity induced by a polyclonal response, as is typical during vaccination.
Although the sequential exposure of antibodies is not likely to occur in this manner
in vivo
, these findings highlight a complication for vaccination, in which nNAbs can interact with the antigen prior to exposure to potential NAb B cell receptor precursors. In this scenario, our results imply that such B-cell receptors may be prevented from interacting with the antigen when exposed to pre-existing nNAbs after injection.
To understand the functional consequence of these antibody combinations on the surface of the sporozoite, we evaluated the extent of the circumsporozoite precipitation reaction (CSPR). CSPR is a well-characterized phenomena for which CSP is secreted at the apical end of sporozoites and then translocated backward, forming a thread-like precipitate at the posterior end of the sporozoite in the presence of anti-CSP Nabs (
Stewart and Vanderberg, 1991
). Incubation of sporozoites with 2F6 and RAM1, either concurrently or by first adding 2F6 resulted in large, well-delineated extensions of CSPR (
Figures 6A
and
6B
). In contrast, when RAM1 was added first, we observed a far-reduced rate of CSPR (
Figures 6A
and
6B
). Interestingly, in sporozoites treated first with RAM1, we observed a different phenomenon. These sporozoite exhibit vesicles that appear to be secreted that measure approximately 300 nm in diameter and are CSP positive. This phenomenon is far less prevalent in sporozoites that have been exposed to 2F6 first or concurrently (
Figures 6A
and
6C
). Together, these data suggest that RAM1 exposure induces an altered state of the sporozoite, potentially rendering it less susceptible to recognition or neutralization by NAbs. As noted above, this relationship could have profound functional consequences for vaccination with attenuated sporozoites in the context of pre-existing nNAbs.
RAM1 reduces protective immunity induced by a subunit CSP vaccine
To alter the outcome of individuals in malaria-endemic areas that have been immunized with a malaria vaccine, pre-existing nNAbs would need to both be effective at impeding the activity of a NAb
in vivo
and diminish the potency of a vaccine-induced polyclonal response
in vivo
. To evaluate whether RAM1 could interfere in the
in vivo
setting of CSP immunization, live infection challenge, we immunized BALB/cJ mice with recombinant
Py
CSP[NXA] and then again 2 and 6 weeks after the initial immunization. After the final immunization, 500 μg 50C1 or RAM1 was passively transferred to mice to mimic an excess of nNAbs at the time of challenge. Twenty-four hours following passive transfer, circulating antibody levels of RAM1 and 50C1 were assessed prior to challenge by the bite of
P. yoelii
-infected
Anopheles
mosquitoes. Approximately 200 μg/ml of RAM1 and 50C1 were detected in the blood prior to challenge (
Figure S4
). Patency was assessed daily beginning 3 days post-challenge. Immunization with NXA resulted in ~80% sterile protection; 70% of NXA-immunized mice that received the non-binding 50C1 control mAb were protected against the blood-stage infection. Strikingly, only ~25% of NXA-immunized mice that received RAM1 were protected from blood-stage infection (
Figure 6D
;
Table S4
).
These findings suggest that RAM1 lessens the neutralization capacity of monoclonal NAbs and can drastically diminish the levels of protection mediated by the polyclonal anti-CSP response elicited by vaccination
in vivo
in a setting analogous to vaccination in the field.
DISCUSSION
Pre-existing humoral immunity is the sum total of many different antibodies, with genetic makeup, epitope specificity, and binding characteristics all contributing to the specific features of the interaction between vaccine-elicited antibodies and their pathogen target. It was suggested decades ago that mAbs had a greater capacity to block infection than polyclonal responses in mice (
Charoenvit et al., 1991
), consistent with the field observation that individuals with naturally occurring polyclonal responses to CSP are not reliably protected from subsequent infection (
Offeddu et al., 2012
). Although it is tempting to characterize antibodies as simply neutralizing or non-neutralizing, embedded within this portrayal is the assumption that antibodies act independently. Rather, our data suggest that the activity of NAbs can be altered by antibodies that, on their own, neither boost nor inhibit infection.
Interestingly, the capacity of RAM1 to reduce the neutralizing activity of 2F6 cannot be explained by a simple assessment of affinity or specificity. Although 2F6 binds to
Py
CSP[NXA] with nanomolar affinity of 1.202 × 10
−9
M (
Figures 1C
and
2B
), RAM1 binds to
Py
CSP[NXA] with less affinity (~2.66 × 10
−8
M) (
Figures 1C
and
2A
). Moreover, RAM1 binds the
Py
CSP[NXA] major repeat region (QGPGAP), whereas 2F6 binds the
Py
CSP [NXA] minor repeat region (QQPP) (
Figure 3D
). From these data alone, we would not predict that RAM1 could outcompete the binding or functionality of 2F6.
However, a more detailed evaluation of the binding of each antibody suggests the potential for a complex interplay between the two molecules on the sporozoite surface, which contains a dense array of
Py
CSP molecules including many major and minor repeats. Our data suggest that 2F6 likely associates with
Py
CSP in a 1:1 binding model, consisting of fast k
on
and very slow k
off
rates. In contrast, RAM1 also exhibits fast k
on
binding kinetics, but a much faster k
off
than 2F6, consistent with a higher stoichiometry of binding. When antibodies were tested for binding as Fabs, RAM1 binding was dramatically reduced, consistent with the hypothesis that avidity is the major driver of RAM1 binding and stability. We predict that these disparate modes of binding facilitate competition between multiple RAM1 molecules and a single 2F6 molecule on the surface of the sporozoite. Indeed, when we expose
Py
sporozoites or
Py
CSP[NXA] to both antibodies, we observe binding of both antibodies to sporozoites rather than saturation of 2F6 (
Figures 2C
and
3E
). Importantly, this competition also has functional consequences; when RAM1 is added prior to 2F6- or
Py
CSP[NXA]-vaccinated BALB/cJ serum, or in higher concentration, it can abrogate the neutralizing function of the NAb 2F6 and serum from immunized mice (
Figure 5
). Thus, avid binding of RAM1 to surface CSP (whether inter- or intra-molecular) appears to interfere with the high affinity binding and neutralization of 2F6, despite the significantly lower affinity of RAM1 for CSP.
Although our experiments were performed in a laboratory setting and focused on direct interference, it is tempting to speculate how inter-antibody interactions may affect VE in the field. Individuals in malaria-endemic areas have anti-CSP antibodies, originating from anti-CSP B cells, that do not achieve sterile protection from infection (
Hoffman et al., 2002
;
Roestenberg et al., 2009
). These anti-CSP B cells receive continual re-stimulation by natural exposure and are likely preferentially boosted by the administration of a CSP-based vaccine like RTS,S/AS01. It stands to reason that this process produces a robust population of anti-CSP nNAbs. Even if this occurs in parallel with the priming and boosting of new protective antibodies during vaccination, the polyclonal response will be a compilation of antibodies, namely, some that may potentiate the activity of others. Although it would be a reasonable hypothesis that antibodies that shared binding epitopes may have the greatest likelihood of competing, our data suggest that the nNAb RAM1, which does not share an epitope with the NAb 2F6, can still diminish the neutralization capacity of the Nab (
Figure 6
).
We hypothesize that the binding of RAM1 to CSP prevents sufficient binding of 2F6 to neutralize sporozoite invasion and/or traversal. (
Figure 7
). Our findings indicate that this interference phenotype of nNAbs affects hepatocyte entry only when pre-exposed, allowing RAM1 to develop the stable avid binding prior to 2F6, or when in molar excess, creating favorable kinetics for RAM1 over 2F6. We note that RAM1 inhibits the traversal and CSP shedding activity of 2F6 without a sequential or escalated dose, indicating that those anti-
Plasmodium
activities which may be more relevant during the time the sporozoite spends in the dermis are likely susceptible to interference by nNAbs.
Direct interference between nNAbs and NAbs at the sporozoite surface represent only one of many challenges that exist to vaccination in the context of pre-existing immunity. In addition to playing a role at the time of sporozoite challenge, which we explore here, nNAbs could also directly bind the vaccine antigen after injection but prior to B cell recognition. Our findings imply that in cases like RAM1, this initial interaction may be able to prevent the NAb B cell precursor from recognizing CSP and becoming stimulated, preventing the generation of robust NAbs. Furthermore, nNAbs may represent original antigenic sin (
Bastos et al., 2007
;
Francis, 1960
;
Kim et al., 2009
;
Sedova et al., 2019
; reviewed in
Vatti et al., 2017
), for which nNAb MBCs are preferentially used by the immune system in response to vaccination. New potential NAb precursor B cells may be at a competitive disadvantage, resulting in a reduced ability to induce potent NAbs. Thus, vaccination may result in a boosting of pre-existing nNAbs and a relative paucity of new NAbs. As shown in this study, this imbalance could directly lead to reduced VE through antibody interference. Thus, deciphering the immunological consequences of pre-existing immunity on VE is an important area for future investigation.
There are threads of evidence in the literature to suggest the presence of antibody interference in the field (
Jongo et al., 2018
;
Sissoko et al., 2017
). The most clinically advanced malaria vaccine RTS,S/AS01 induced 50%–87% sterile efficacy in controlled human malaria infection studies (
Gordon et al., 1995
;
Kester et al., 2008
;
Regules et al., 2016
). However, in phase III clinical trials of pediatric subjects in malaria-endemic regions, RTS,S/AS01 did not induce sterile protection, but rather a ~30% partial protection was achieved. The heterogeneity in CSP haplotype in the field had an effect on VE of RTS,S/AS01 (
Neafsey et al., 2015
;
Pringle et al., 2018
), but it does not account for the complete lack of sterilizing immunity. Thus, achieving sterile efficacy against malaria infection in non-immune western adults does not translate to protection in pre-immune subjects in malaria-endemic areas. The mechanisms by which pre-existing immunity reduces VE and the key factors influencing poor efficacy of vaccine-induced immunity are largely unknown, constituting a key roadblock to overcome along the road to eliminate malaria.
Despite extensive vector control efforts, highly effective anti-malarial drugs, and several vaccine candidates that have shown promise in malaria-naive individuals, malaria remains a global health problem worldwide. It is widely appreciated that a highly effective vaccine in malaria-endemic populations would contribute dramatically to malaria eradication. Yet, malaria vaccine development efforts continue to suffer from a severe disconnect between promising VE in malaria-naive westerners and a lack of sterilizing VE in people in endemic regions. It is well-recognized that pre-existing immunity to malaria is a key roadblock to the development of an effective vaccine (
Good, 1995
). Our work demonstrates that antibody interference between nNAbs and NAbs (
Figure 7
) may contribute to this lack of translatability in endemic populations. Future work will interrogate the importance of antibody interference in tuning VE against human-infectious malaria. A better understanding of the mechanisms by which vaccines fail to induce robust protection in malaria-endemic areas could inform next-generation vaccines and help to control malaria worldwide.
LIMITATIONS OF STUDY
Our study establishes a proof of principle that non-neutralizing anti-CSP antibodies can hamper the protective efficacy of NAbs to CSP in a rodent model. Although both
Py
and
Pf
CSP repeat regions contain two distinct repeat motifs in tandem, their primary organization and sequence differ. Given these differences, it remains to be determined whether this phenomenon extends to human-infectious malarias and, if so, whether any molecular details are conserved. In
P. yoelii
infection of BALB/cJ mice, high levels of antibody (above what is seen in protected humans in the field) are required to achieve a consistent experimental readout of protection against sporozoite challenge. It is therefore possible that our proof of concept is influenced by these supraphysiological conditions. Yet, these models have inherent value as surrogates for dissecting immunity against the parasite, allowing us to understand phenomena that otherwise cannot be studied. Finally, our study is limited in that it describes only a single instance of antibody interference; the characterization of additional mAbs will reveal the extent and molecular details of antibody interference altering neutralization.

Experimental animals

Mosquito rearing and sporozoite production
P. yoelii
wild-type strain 17XNL (BEI resources) was maintained in Swiss Webster mice (Envigo). Swiss Webster mice were injected intraperitoneal (IP) with 250 μL of infected blood at 3%–5% parasitemia. Mice were then anesthetized with 150 μL Ketamine Xylazine solution (12.5 mg/mL ketamine, 1.25 mg/mL xylazine in PBS) and naive female Anopheles stephensi mosquitoes (3–7 days old) were allowed to feed on them. Mosquitoes were maintained at 23°C and 80% humidity with a 12L-12D light cycle. On day 10, the midguts from ten mosquitoes are dissected and oocysts counted as a measure of infection. On day 15 post-infection, mosquitoes are used for mosquito bite challenge or are dissected to isolate salivary glands and extract sporozoites.

Mosquito Bite Challenge
Mice were anesthetized by IP injection of 150 μL Ketamine/Xylazine solution (12.5 mg/mL ketamine, 1.25 mg/mL xylazine in PBS). Once anesthetized, pairs of mice were each placed on a carton of 15 infectious mosquitoes and mosquitoes allowed to bite through the mesh top for 10 mins. Every thirty seconds mice were rotated among mosquito cartons to ensure equal exposure of mice and to maximize mosquito probing. Mice received subcutaneous PBS injections and recovered from anesthesia under a heat lamp. Mice were checked for the presence of blood stage parasites (patency) beginning 4 days post-challenge.
